data.title: Procopius writes about the Slavs in the 6th century
data.excerpt: Procopius of Caesarea (c. 500 – c. 565) spent fifteen full years on the staff of the Byzantine general Belisarius and met the Slavs in person on campaign. His account of their one God, their wretched huts, their shields and spears and their appearance is among the earliest detailed descriptions of the Slavs left by an ancient author.

children.text: Procopius (c. 500 – c. 565) was an important Byzantine historian and scholar, known above all for his work on the Byzantine–Persian, Byzantine–Vandal and Byzantine–Ostrogothic wars during the reign of Emperor Justinian I. He was born around the year 500 in the wealthy port city of Caesarea. He was a Palestinian, and the administration of the whole province had its seat in his city. His mother tongue was Greek and he commanded Latin as well. Besides that he knew Syriac, spoke Persian well and even understood Gothic. He was educated in the famous school of rhetoric in Gaza and later broadened his education in the legal sciences. It was above all his employment that widened his horizons. For fifteen full years he was an adviser on the staff of the famous Byzantine general Belisarius. In that position he took part in several campaigns, on which he came into direct contact with the Slavs. He then returned to Constantinople, survived the great plague and began to write the history of the reign of Emperor Justinian. He lived and worked in a setting where all the serious reports from the empire of the day came together. That is why his information is very reliable. Procopius was also a conscientious historian. He made a great many notes, and if official documents came into his hands, he made copies and extracts from them. It is with him, among the first of the ancient authors, that we meet a more detailed description of the Slavs in the period of the 6th century.
Let us then read an extract from his work in which he briefly described the life of the Slavs (Hyper tón polemón logoi, that is, The Wars, Book III, chapter 14 (the years 530–545)):

blocks.text:
As soon as that news spread, almost all the Antes gathered,  for they thought it a matter concerning the whole community. They supposed that they would gain great advantage from having seized Chilbudius, the commander of the Roman army. These tribes, that is the Slavs and the Antes, are not subject to a single man, but from of old they live in a democracy, and therefore they deliberate in common on their affairs, both the favourable and the unfavourable. Likewise all the other customs of these barbarian tribes have long been alike. They believe that there is one God, the maker of thunder and the sole lord of all things, and they sacrifice to him oxen and animals of every kind. They know nothing of relentless fate, nor in the end do they ascribe to it any influence upon men. When their death draws near — whether they fall ill or go to war — they vow to God that they will bring him a thanksgiving offering if they do not perish; and when they escape, they sacrifice to him what they promised, and imagine that they have bought back their life at the price of this offering.
They also revere rivers, water nymphs and other deities, they sacrifice to them all, and at these sacrifices they read omens. They dwell in wretched huts, set far apart from one another, and they move continually from place to place. If they march to battle, most of them go on foot against the enemy; in their hands they carry small shields and spears, but they wear no body armour. Some have neither shirt nor cloak, but put on only trousers drawn up to the waist, and so they go out to fight against the enemy. Both tribes have a single language, and a wholly barbarian one. Nor do they differ from one another in appearance in any way. They are all of tall and strong build. The colour of their skin is not very white, the colour of their hair is not very fair and does not pass entirely into black either, but they are all brownish. They lead a harsh and primitive life, just as the Massagetae do, and like them they are always full of filth. They are not, however, malicious or treacherous, and in their simplicity they preserve the Hunnic way of life. Even the name of the Slavs and the Antes was one and the same in the past. Both alike were in truth called Sporoi, perhaps because they dwell scattered in tents — sporadically. For this reason too they have much land, for the greatest part of the bank on the far side of the Danube is settled.
